---
title: "5. Simulate, fit, check"
description: >
  Data simulated from known parameters at the survey design of tutorial 1:
  does the fit recover the truth, and are its intervals honest?
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 110,
                      out.width = "100%")
library(ggplot2)
# site builds: GADM files downloaded earlier, if STAREAL_GADM_CACHE names a folder of them
local({
  cache <- Sys.getenv("STAREAL_GADM_CACHE")
  if (nzchar(cache)) {
    dir.create(file.path(tempdir(), "gadm"), showWarnings = FALSE)
    file.copy(list.files(cache, pattern = "^gadm41_", full.names = TRUE), file.path(tempdir(), "gadm"))
  }
})
```

With real data, the truth is unknown, and a model can only be judged by how
well it predicts ([tutorial 4](crossval.html)). With simulated data, the
truth is known, so the fit can be checked against it directly. This is
worth doing for your own design before trusting a map. Can these surveys,
in these places and months, identify the parameters? How wide should the
intervals be where there are no data?

This tutorial simulates data at the survey design of
[tutorial 1](crt76t.html): the same area-months, with the same numbers
tested. It fits the model, and compares the result with the truth, first
for one simulation and then over twenty.

```{r packages}
library(stareal)
```

## 1. Simulating at a real design

`simulate_areal()` draws one surface from the model and then binomial
surveys. Given `cells`, it surveys those area-time cells with their numbers
tested. The `$cells` of real data qualifies, so a simulation can copy a real
design:

```{r design, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE}
iso3 <- c("DJI", "ERI", "ETH", "KEN", "SOM", "SSD", "SDN", "UGA")
adm1 <- sf::st_as_sf(geodata::gadm(iso3, level = 1, path = tempdir(), version = "4.1", resolution = 2))
lakes <- rnaturalearth::ne_download(scale = 10, type = "lakes", category = "physical",
                                    returnclass = "sf", destdir = tempdir())
crs <- "+proj=laea +lat_0=8 +lon_0=37 +units=m"
adm1 <- sf::st_make_valid(sf::st_transform(adm1, crs))
lakes <- sf::st_make_valid(sf::st_transform(lakes, crs))
lakes <- lakes[as.numeric(sf::st_area(lakes)) > 1e9, ]
water <- sf::st_intersection(sf::st_union(lakes), sf::st_union(adm1))
adm1 <- sf::st_difference(adm1, water)
adm1 <- adm1[adm1$ENGTYPE_1 != "Water body", ]           # what is left of Uganda's lake units
fr <- areal_frame(adm1, id = "GID_1", groups = c(country = "COUNTRY"), link_within = "country",
                  verbose = FALSE)
tf <- time_frame(1989, 2024, "month")
d <- areal_data(igad_crt76t, fr, tf, y = "positive", k = "tested",
                coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), date = "collection_day", verbose = FALSE)
```

The parameters are of the same order as tutorial 1's posterior: a strong
field, smooth in space and time, and a declining trend.

```{r simulate}
sim <- simulate_areal(fr, tf, cells = d$cells, sigma = 3, rho_s = 0.97, rho_t = 0.997,
                      sigma_n = 0.6, beta = c(intercept = 0.5, trend = -2), seed = 101)
sim
```

The simulation is an ordinary data object, with the truth attached:
`sim$truth$prevalence` is the prevalence of every area in every month.

```{r truth-map, fig.height = 4}
truth_map <- function(month) {
  m <- sf::st_sf(id = adm1$GID_1, geometry = sf::st_geometry(adm1))
  m$prevalence <- sim$truth$prevalence[m$id, month]
  m$time <- month
  m
}
tm <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("1995-07", "2010-07", "2024-07"), truth_map))
ggplot(tm) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = prevalence), colour = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = sf::st_sf(water), fill = "#bcd6ea", colour = NA) +
  facet_wrap(~time) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c("true\nprevalence", limits = c(0, 1), option = "magma") +
  theme_void()
```

## 2. Fitting

The same call as for real data:

```{r fit, message = FALSE}
fit <- fit_areal(sim)
diagnose(fit)$checks
```

## 3. The parameters against the truth

```{r params}
tab <- summary(fit)$table[, c("variable", "mean", "q2.5", "q97.5")]
tab$truth <- c(sim$truth$theta, sim$truth$beta)[tab$variable]
tab$covered <- tab$q2.5 <= tab$truth & tab$truth <= tab$q97.5
tab
```

```{r missed, include = FALSE}
missed <- tab$variable[!tab$covered]
```

`r sum(tab$covered)` of the `r nrow(tab)` intervals cover their true
values`r if (length(missed)) paste0("; the misses are ", paste(missed, collapse = ", ")) else ""`.
One simulation is one draw, though. Whether misses like these are bad luck
or a pattern is the job of the repeated study in section 5.

## 4. The surface against the truth

The parameters are a means to an end; the map is what gets used.
`predict()` gives every area-month, and each can be checked against the true
prevalence:

```{r surface}
pr <- predict(fit, verbose = FALSE)
pr$area$truth <- sim$truth$prevalence[cbind(pr$area$id, pr$area$time)]
pr$area$covered <- pr$area$q2.5 <= pr$area$truth & pr$area$truth <= pr$area$q97.5
pr$area$surveyed <- ifelse(pr$area$k > 0, "surveyed area-months", "unsurveyed area-months")
aggregate(cbind(covered, width = q97.5 - q2.5) ~ surveyed, pr$area, mean)
```

```{r surface-plot, fig.height = 4.5}
ggplot(pr$area, aes(truth, mean)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.15, size = 0.6) +
  geom_abline(colour = "red") +
  facet_wrap(~surveyed) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "true prevalence", y = "posterior mean") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r surface-numbers, include = FALSE}
cs <- aggregate(cbind(covered, width = q97.5 - q2.5) ~ surveyed, pr$area, mean)
ratio <- cs$width[cs$surveyed == "unsurveyed area-months"] / cs$width[cs$surveyed == "surveyed area-months"]
```

Where there are surveys, the posterior mean follows the truth closely and
the intervals are narrow. Where there are none, which is most area-months
(only `r length(unique(d$cells$area))` of the `r fr$m` units have any
data), the estimates shrink toward the regional mean. Many unsurveyed
units are far from it, so the means scatter widely. But their intervals
are about `r round(ratio)` times as wide, and still cover the truth about as
often as they should.

The coverage of one simulation moves with its estimated parameters, which
all its cells share. Section 5 averages over twenty simulations.

## 5. Over twenty simulations

One simulation is one draw: a parameter outside its interval might be bad
luck. The way to know is to repeat the exercise many times, with new
surfaces and surveys at the same design. That is twenty fits and twenty
predictions, too long for a tutorial, so it was run once with the code
above in a loop (`data-raw/simulation_crt76t.R` in the source repository),
keeping each parameter's interval and the surface's coverage. The results
ship with *stareal*:

```{r study-import}
study <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "simulation_crt76t.rds", package = "stareal"))
params <- study$params
params$covered <- params$q2.5 <= params$truth & params$truth <= params$q97.5
aggregate(covered ~ variable, params, mean)
```

```{r study-params, fig.height = 4.5}
ggplot(params, aes(rep, mean, ymin = q2.5, ymax = q97.5, colour = covered)) +
  geom_pointrange(size = 0.2) +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = truth), linetype = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~variable, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "grey30", `FALSE` = "red")) +
  labs(x = "simulation", y = "posterior mean and 95% interval", colour = "covers the truth") +
  theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r study-surface}
aggregate(cbind(covered, width) ~ observed, study$surface, mean)
```

```{r study-counts, include = FALSE}
n_cov <- tapply(params$covered, params$variable, sum)
n_sim <- length(unique(params$rep))
above <- function(v) with(params[params$variable == v & !params$covered, ], sum(truth > q97.5))
miss <- function(v) n_sim - n_cov[[v]]
n_pass <- sum(tapply(params$pass, params$rep, all))
```

With twenty simulations, an honest 95% interval misses the truth about once,
and two or three misses are not unusual. Over the twenty:

- `sigma` and `sigma_n` cover the truth `r n_cov[["sigma"]]` and
  `r n_cov[["sigma_n"]]` times.
- `rho_s` covers it `r n_cov[["rho_s"]]` times and `rho_t`
  `r n_cov[["rho_t"]]` times. Their misses all fall on the same side: the
  truth is just above the interval (`r above("rho_s")` of
  `r miss("rho_s")` for `rho_s`, `r above("rho_t")` of `r miss("rho_t")` for
  `rho_t`). Both truths are close to 1. How close a correlation is to 1 is
  decided by a few broad patterns, which these data see only dimly, so the
  posterior leans toward the prior's mass further from 1.
- The `intercept` and the `trend` cover the truth `r n_cov[["intercept"]]`
  and `r n_cov[["trend"]]` times, with misses on both sides. The regional
  level and slope trade off against the field's own region-wide component,
  whose variance is proportional to `sigma^2 / (1 - rho_s)`. When `rho_s`
  is estimated too low, that variance is understated, and the fit is too
  sure of the regional level and slope.
- The surface, which is what the maps are made of, covers the truth in
  about 94% of area-months, surveyed or not (the table above).
- `diagnose()` passed `r n_pass` of the `r n_sim` fits at the default
  length. Check every fit: a fit that fails needs a longer run.

Is something wrong? Not with the software. A Bayesian 95% interval is
calibrated on average over the prior, not at every fixed truth, and a truth
near the edge of what the data can resolve is where it can under-cover.
Simulation-based calibration ([Talts et al. 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1804.06788))
checks the software itself. It draws the parameters from the prior,
simulates, fits, and checks that the truth's rank among the posterior
draws is uniform. For *stareal*, 200 such simulations on a small lattice
gave uniform ranks for every parameter (`data-raw/check_sbc.R` in the
source repository).

The lesson for this design: the surface's intervals can be taken at face
value. The correlations, and the regional intercept read as a result in
its own right, are less certain than their intervals say when the
correlations are close to 1. A simulation at your own design, like this
one, shows whether that applies to you.

## 6. What this does and does not show

A simulation from the model itself checks the software and the design:
that the sampler finds the posterior, and that these surveys can identify
the parameters. It cannot show that the model suits real data. The
simulated field is exactly the model's field, with the same smoothness
everywhere, no outliers and no study effects.

Two extensions make the check harder and more useful:

- **Simulate from something else** and fit the model to it: a localised
  emergence like that of [tutorial 2](k13-561h.html), a covariate the fit
  leaves out, or overdispersed surveys. The question then is whether the
  intervals stay honest when the model is wrong.
- **Simulate a design you are planning**: add the surveys you might
  collect to `cells`, and see how much the intervals in the unsurveyed
  areas shrink.
